summary: For ages 5–7 (Animal Homes): children learn that animals MAKE or FIND many kinds of home (nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge), that each home has a JOB — shelter from weather and predators and a safe place for young — and can match common animals to their homes. The central activity is an active animal↔home match where a correct match reveals the animal and its babies sheltered inside, plus a BUILT-vs-FOUND sort. Supporting scaffolds (tap-to-reveal cutaway scenes and a short recognition check) and a hands-on 'gather natural materials' step are included to make 'home = protection' concrete and to distinguish the specific home from the wider habitat.
misconceptions: Thinking every animal builds its own home — missing that some FIND or borrow one (the hermit crab uses a cast-off shell; some animals shelter in existing holes).
Believing a home is just 'where the animal sits/lives', not grasping its job as protection and a safe place for babies.
Assuming animals build like people do (with tools or bought materials) rather than from natural materials (mud, twigs, wax, silk).
Over-generalising one home type ('all animals live in nests') to every animal.
Confusing a whole HABITAT (the woodland, the pond) with the animal's specific HOME (its nest, its burrow) within that habitat.

activities.title: Take each animal home (match and peek inside)
steps: Look at a scene with several places — a tree, a grassy bank, a pond, a garden corner and a seashore rock pool — and a row of animals waiting to go home.

Match each animal to its home: bird→nest (in the tree), rabbit→burrow (in the grassy bank), bee→hive (in a hollow in the tree), spider→web (in the garden corner), hermit crab→shell (in the seashore rock pool), fox→den (in the bank), beaver→lodge (in the pond).

On a correct match, look inside the opened/cutaway home to see how it protects the animal (eggs warm in the nest, kits deep in the burrow, cubs in the den, bee grubs in the wax cells). Not every home holds babies: the hermit crab's shell protects its soft body, and a spider's web mainly catches food, with eggs kept in a silk egg sac.
Say out loud what the home is for — e.g. 'it keeps them warm', 'it hides them from danger'.
When a match is wrong, notice the animal won't fit and try a different home.
activities.insight: A home is not just where an animal sits — it is shelter that protects the animal, and many homes also keep babies safe; different animals have different homes.

activities.title: Built or found? (a sorting surprise)
steps: Sort the homes into two groups: ones the animal BUILT (nest, web, hive — bees build the wax comb, often inside a hollow they found — lodge, burrow) and ones it FOUND or borrowed (the hermit crab's empty shell; an animal sheltering in a hollow log).
Explain for one or two examples how it was made or found — a bird gathers twigs and grass; a hermit crab backs into an empty shell left behind by a sea snail.
Talk about the surprise that not every animal makes its own home.
activities.insight: Some animals build their home and some find or borrow one — so 'animals have homes' does not mean 'every animal builds a nest'.

activities.title: Explore the habitat scene (tap to peek inside)
steps: Explore a habitat picture spanning land, water and high places (underground burrow, treetop nest, beaver lodge in a pond with an underwater entrance and a dry room above the water, garden web).
Tap a place — the tree, the ground, the pond — to open a cutaway of the home with the animal and its young inside.
Read or hear a one-line 'what it's for' and point to where the babies are kept safe.
activities.insight: Animals live in homes all around us — underground, up in trees and bushes, and in and beside water — and each cutaway shows the animal sheltered inside.

activities.title: Build like an animal does (natural materials)
steps: Gather pretend or real natural materials to make a simple home — twigs and grass for a nest, sticks and mud for a lodge.
Name the material for each home: nest = twigs & grass, hive = wax, web = silk, lodge = sticks & mud.
Notice that animals build from what nature provides — no shops, no bought tools.
activities.insight: Animals build with natural materials they find, not with tools or materials bought from shops the way people do.

activities.title: Home vs whole place, and who makes it (talk check)
steps: Answer: 'A bird's nest and your house are both called homes. What is a nest FOR — what does it do for the bird? And who makes a bird's nest?'

Answer follow-ups: Why do many birds build a nest when they lay eggs? Does a bird stay in its nest all day and night the way you stay in your house? Where is a rabbit's home — up a tree or under the ground, and why? Did the hermit crab build its shell or find it?
Point to the specific home (the nest) versus the wider place the animal lives in (the forest, the garden).
activities.insight: A home is the specific shelter that protects the animal and its young, which the animal builds or finds itself — different from the whole habitat it lives in.

checkQuestion: A bird's nest and your house are both called 'homes'. What is a nest FOR — what does it do for the bird? And who makes a bird's nest?
checkAnswer: The nest is for shelter and protection — a safe place to lay eggs and keep the chicks warm and hidden from predators and weather. The bird itself builds the nest, gathering twigs, grass and moss; people do not make it for the bird.
